opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was a very real constraint for us. When I started, the naive plan was: let's pretrain our own small model from scratch, control everything, and study safety properties end to end. Then we did the math on compute, and even a model that's tiny by industry standards was going to eat up most of what our lab could realistically get. And one training run is never one training run. You need ablations, you need to redo things when you find a bug. So that plan just didn't survive contact with the budget.

So we shifted in a few ways. The first was to stop treating pretraining as the place where an academic group adds value. Industry labs are always going to win on that axis. Instead we asked: what questions can you answer by working *on top of* existing open-weight models? That pushed us toward fine-tuning, alignment, and especially evaluation and red-teaming, where the expensive part has already been paid for by someone else, and the interesting scientific questions are about behavior: how safety alignment can be undone, how robust it is, what goes wrong when you adapt a model downstream.

The second shift was methodological. We got much more disciplined about designing experiments that are cheap but still informative. Small-scale fine-tuning, parameter-efficient methods, careful controlled comparisons rather than brute-force scaling. You learn to ask, "What's the minimum experiment that would actually change my mind?" That constraint, honestly, made the research sharper.

And the third thing was choosing problems where insight matters more than scale. For example, it turned out that a surprisingly small amount of fine-tuning could erode a model's safety guardrails. You don't need a supercomputer to show that, but it's an important finding for the whole field. So in a way, the compute limit forced us into an area that ended up being both feasible and quite impactful.

Looking back, I wouldn't say it was a compromise. It was more like the constraint helped us find where academia can actually contribute something that the big labs either can't or won't do themselves.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, that was a pretty humbling moment for us. When we started, the plan was straightforward: pretrain a small model ourselves, maybe a few hundred million parameters, so we could control the data and really study what was happening inside. Then we actually priced it out. Even at that scale, the compute for a proper training run, plus all the ablations you'd need to say anything meaningful, was far beyond what an academic group like ours could afford. And it's not just the money. If a run takes two weeks and you only get a handful of them, every mistake costs you a month.

So we had to be honest with ourselves about where our advantage actually was. It wasn't in scale, and it never would be. Industry labs will always have more GPUs. So the question became: what can we learn without owning the whole training process?

We shifted in a few directions. First, we leaned heavily on open-weight models and open checkpoints. Things like Pythia, OLMo, and later the Qwen and Llama families gave us intermediate checkpoints and, in some cases, the actual training data. That let us study training dynamics after the fact rather than reproducing them. Second, we went much smaller, almost embarrassingly small. Toy settings, tens of millions of parameters, synthetic data where we controlled every variable. People sometimes laugh at that, but you can test a hypothesis in an afternoon, and a surprising number of phenomena show up at that scale if you design the task well. Third, we moved more of our effort toward post-training and evaluation, where a single GPU or a few hours of API credits gets you real results.

The thing I'd say to students is that the constraint actually sharpened our thinking. When you can't brute-force anything, you're forced to ask much more precise questions. Some of our best papers came out of that period, precisely because we had to find the cheapest experiment that could still change someone's mind.

I shifted toward questions I could investigate using existing models and smaller experiments. That meant being more precise about what I wanted to learn, and designing experiments around that rather than around building a model. The constraint changed the research plan, but it didn’t mean I had to stop doing research.
